Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 45-year-old man of African descent, currently in a long-term relationship and working as an agricultural laborer on a large farm. He presents with a quiet, guarded demeanor, his large frame often held rigidly still. He speaks in a low, deliberate voice, and his eyes frequently drift to the floor, as if scanning for something unseen.

He was born in a rural village in his home country, the eldest of five children. He describes his father as a "hard man," a farmer who worked from dawn until dusk. But the work was not the hardest part. The hardest part began when the sun went down. From as early as he can remember, from the age of perhaps five or six, he would lie in the dark, listening. The sounds were predictable: the heavy thud of his father's boots on the dirt floor, the sharp, rising pitch of his mother's voice, then the crack of a hand against flesh, followed by her weeping. He learned to identify the specific sounds of violence-the scrape of a chair being shoved, the thump of a body hitting a wall, the sickening, wet sound of a blow.

He never saw it, not directly. He would pull the thin blanket over his head, squeezing his eyes shut, trying to will his body to become a stone, to not exist. He felt a profound, suffocating helplessness. He remembers the smell of kerosene from the lamp, the taste of bile in his throat, and the desperate, silent prayer that he would simply disappear. The next morning, his father would be silent, his mother would move stiffly, and the world would pretend the night never happened. Mr. A. learned to do the same. He buried the fear, the rage, the shame of his own inaction, so deep he could almost forget it was there.

Now, decades later, he lives in a small, tidy apartment with his partner, a woman he has been with for twelve years. He works from sunrise to late afternoon, stooping over rows of lettuce and strawberries. The physical exhaustion is a comfort; it quiets his mind. But the past is never truly buried. It surfaces in the unexpected quiet of his commute home, the engine of his old truck humming a low drone. A sudden, sharp sound-a car backfiring, a dropped crate in the warehouse-will send a jolt through him, his heart hammering against his ribs, his palms slick with sweat. He will scan the parking lot, his body coiled, ready to fight or flee, even though there is no threat.

At home, he is a ghost. He cannot sit with his partner and watch television. The intimacy of the couch, the soft lighting, it feels too vulnerable. He prefers the hard chair in the corner of the kitchen, his back to the wall, where he can see both doors. He has not spoken of his childhood to her. When she asks what is wrong, he says, "I am just tired. The sun was hot." He has a deep, unshakeable feeling that he is dangerous, that the same violence he witnessed is coiled inside him, waiting. He avoids conflict with an almost pathological vigilance. If his partner raises her voice in frustration, even about a minor thing like a misplaced bill, he goes silent, his face becoming a mask. Inside, he is five years old again, frozen, listening.

He sleeps in fits, often waking with a start, his body drenched in sweat, the phantom sounds of his childhood ringing in his ears. He has nightmares, not of his father, but of being trapped in a small, dark space, unable to move or cry out. He has begun to drink more in the evenings-a few beers, then a few more-to dull the hyper-vigilance, to quiet the constant, low-level hum of dread that lives in his chest. The farm, with its wide, open fields, is the only place he feels a measure of safety, because he can see everything, and no one can sneak up on him. He is a man who has spent forty years trying to outrun a darkness he never saw, but has felt every single day.
